newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Religious police crack down in Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Religious police crack down in Kabul.

text.p: The Taleban's religious police have tightened regulations in Kabul, punishing 700 travellers for trimming their beards and beating at least two female doctors according to Taleban radio and international aid workers in Kabul.

"Seven hundred passengers who were travelling on the Kabul to Kandahar (in southern Afghanistan) highway were punished in accordance with Islamic law for trimming or cutting their beards," said a broadcast on Taleban-controlled Radio Shariat on Tuesday night.
The department was acting on orders of the acting Minister of Justice, Mullah Nurudddin Turabi, according to the report.

The Taleban's religious police, formally known as the Ama bin Marouf wa Nahi al Munkar (Department for Prevention of Vice and Promotion of Virtue), has decreed that men should not shave or trim their beards. The decree says a beard must be long enough to protrude from a fist clenched at the base of the chin.
The Radio Shariat report did not say how the beard-trimmers were punished.
There has been at least one incident involving the religious police beating female medical staff at the hospital where they worked, according to aid workers in Kabul.

No one directly involved in the incident was willing to comment, but an aid worker said it came on top of decrees from the religious police that will increase difficulties faced by international aid workers trying to deliver medical and other aid to Kabul's hard-pressed populace.
When the Taleban arrived in Kabul last September, they banned women from working outside the home, except in the medical sector.

But even there they are subject to restrictions on what they can wear and whom they can see. On July 16 the religious police issued a decree restating those restrictions and introducing further limitations.

"Women are not allowed to work in any field except the medical sector. Aid agencies need to gain permission from the Department for Promoting Virtue and Preventing Vice to employ or assist women," says the July 16 decree, which was distributed to aid agencies and hospitals in Kabul.
"The Islamic law of our country does not allow the employment of women in government departments or international agencies. Women should not go outside their residences," say the regulations.
Care International, one of the world's largest aid agencies, suspended its programmes in Kabul after the regulations were issued.
Care believes that compliance with the regulations as stated would make it impossible to continue distributing food aid to widows -- one of its major programmes -- and be against its principles.

"(Our programmes) are temporarily suspended since these regulations make the food distribution operationally impossible, and are an attempt to cause Care to break with its core values." said Stuart Worsley of Care on Wednesday.

"Care does and cannot distinguish between people in need according to gender, race, social status or political standing. For Care to continue to provide assistance to men and not to women would go against our principles," said Worsley.

Further items in the decree banned women from wearing jewellery and make-up; from making a noise with their shoes when they walked; and from sitting beside the driver when travelling to and from work.

"Stylish dress and decoration of women in hospitals is forbidden. Women are duty bound to behave with dignity, to walk calmly and refrain from hitting their shoes on the ground, which makes noises," said the decree.
Worsley of Care believes that the regulations can be modified to make them acceptable to both the Taleban and the aid community.

"We have spoken to several ministries and their response has been both encouraging and understanding. They have shown concern: we believe that they are doing what they can to come to some kind of satisfactory solution," said Worsley.
